title: Article III standing
summary: A federal plaintiff must show a concrete personal injury, a sufficient connection between that injury and the challenged conduct, and a likelihood that the requested relief will address the injury.
notes:
Article III standing determines whether the particular claimant has the personal stake needed for a federal court to exercise judicial power over a particular claim and requested remedy. The course text organizes the inquiry into injury in fact, causation, and redressability. Injury must be concrete and particularized and actual or imminent. Causation asks whether the injury is fairly traceable to the challenged conduct. Redressability asks whether a favorable judicial decision is likely to address that injury. The claimant must satisfy each element; the presence of an important public question does not establish them.

The procedural stage matters. Pleading may support a plausible allegation; summary judgment requires evidence supporting standing. Lujan examines affidavits and testimony about future visits to endangered-species habitats. Laidlaw examines actual losses of recreational use connected to ongoing unlawful discharges. Standing must also support each form of relief sought: an injury that supports one remedy does not automatically support another.

Keep constitutional standing separate from the statutory question whether Congress authorized this claimant to sue and from the merits of the legal challenge. ADAPSO rejected an approach that required a plaintiff to prove a legally protected interest before obtaining judicial review. The zone-of-interests inquiry remains an additional question about the statutory scheme. A plaintiff who clears the threshold may still lose on the merits. The cases also distinguish standing at the beginning of a suit from later mootness.
